author: Hans Hauge
title: Cryptoassets Explained: Civic - Civic USD (Cryptocurrency:CVC-USD)
text:
Introduction The Civic ( CVC-USD ) team is taking on the very hairy, but absolutely necessary task of tackling digital identity.
Source: Civic.com
Launched in 2017 by crypto celebrity Vinny Lingham , the Civic team has become one of the top blockchain identity platforms working in the space.
Purpose and Classification If you're not familiar with the problems associated with identity, fasten your seat belt. Let's just cover the broad strokes and get a 30,000-foot view.
Current identity systems rely on central authority, which means that the process is slow, expensive and inefficient (think about taking a number at the DMV). Additionally, fake IDs are easy to obtain and identity theft has been on the rise for years. Computer systems can be used to help solve the identity puzzle, but these come with their own hosts of problems. People change over time, making identification by image recognition challenging. Plus, what happens if you identify someone by their finger print, and then they lose their finger in an accident? Identity is a sensitive issue. While identifying people is necessary to ensure that they do in fact own something, or that they are the party to which something should be delivered, I don't necessarily want my identity broadcast in public at all times. Over-identifying people has the effect of turning normal people into mini celebrities and destroying all their privacy in the process. The most effective identity solutions are still very hard to use for normal people (too technical). For example, using PGP encryption I could sign something proving that it's mine, or that I was indeed the author of a certain message. But very few people understand how to use PGP. Data that's linked to identity is stored in vast information silos at companies like Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) ( GOOGL ), Facebook ( FB ), and many other large companies like Target ( TGT ). When a data breach occurs, our sensitive data is then sold on the black market to the highest bidder. These data silos have become honey pots for hackers, and by the time we find out about a hack, the damage has already been done. Every year we collectively build more digital personas, visit more sites that we need to keep track of, create more passwords to worry about, and we make more data than the year before . This means that unless we find solutions that change the game, these problems could continue to get worse. Financial regulations can be intrusive and expensive. KYC and AML compliance are hot topics right now in the crypto space, but the broader picture comes from financial institutions and money service businesses that have been dealing with this for years. Forbes reports that some companies spend over $500M every year just to maintain compliance. In 2016, 15.4 million people in the United States were affected by identity theft, resulting in losses of $16 billion (an increase from 2015). The most common form of data breach involved access to Personally Identifiable Information, or "PII." In 2016, it was reported that over one billion people in the developing world had no form of legal proof of their identity. Without proper identity documents, many people are not able to have a banking relationship. This results in a huge number of unbanked people globally. In the US alone there are millions of households without access to banking. Simple verification, such as ensuring that someone is 21 years of age or greater, requires someone to hand over their driver's license, passport, or similar document. Invariably, the buyer in this example will have to divulge additional information, such as their street address, if they're an organ donor, etc. All this information is simply printed on their ID. Additionally, knowing the buyer's age is extra information, as long as they are at least 21. What does it matter if they are 22 or 62? However, the only way to verify this is by knowing someone's birthday, which exposes the additional information. This list above is just the tip of the iceberg. We could go on all day about these complications and challenges. The fact is, the world is getting more digital all the time, and we need a solution for digital identity.
So, on the purpose front, I applaud this effort. There is clearly a problem to be solved here.
Taxonomy: Utility Token
Age, History, Current Status Prior to co-founding Civic, CEO Vinny Lingham made a name for himself by starting Gyft, an online platform for buying, selling and sending gift cards. Gyft accepts purchases in Bitcoin ( BTC-USD )( COIN )( OTCQX:GBTC ), which enabled Bitcoin holders to spend their BTC at any of the 200 retailers supported.
The Civic project was announced on the Bitcointalkforum on May 31, 2017. The token sale was a success the following month, raising $33M . The recent listing on Coinbase will certainly be beneficial in the long run, but the market's reaction was muted.
Software Development Civic has apps for both Apple ( AAPL ) and Android platforms. The app on the Google Play store has more than 50k downloads, and a rating of 3.9. On the iTunes store, the app has 4.5 stars, but only 66 ratings .
The Civic GitHub account seems a bit quiet to me. But there are signs of life. The Civic developer documentation looks nice . It's clear that some effort was spent on this. This is generally a good sign.
Source: Civic.com developer docs
Market Capitalization Civic is one of the smaller cryptoassets listed on Coinbase. Coming in with only $19M in market cap, Civic ranks 132nd at the time of this writing over on Coinmarketcap.com
Source: Coinmarketcap.com
Exchange Liquidity Civic is an ERC-20 token, so it can be traded on many decentralized exchanges. Even though the Coinbase listing is currently accepting deposits, at the time of writing, Coinbase Pro trading is not enabled. Currently, the most exchange volume is happening on Binance ( BNB-USD ).
Source: Coinmarketcap.com
Token Issuance Model There are 1,000,000,000 (one billion) Civic tokens in existence. However, there are only 342M in circulation. The total of 1B is the hard cap. There should never be any more tokens issued.
It seems that the recent Coinbase listing didn't do much for the price, which has been beat up this year. Earlier this year, CVC was trading around $1.21, but now you can pick these up for less than $0.06 each.
Source: Coinmarketcap.com
Security The Civic smart contract can be found here . Some of the security for this token comes from the underlying blockchain (Ethereum in this case), but there are a number of security concerns to be considered.
First of all, every encumbrance of PII is coming into play. Secondly, the providers and attestation reports have to be airtight.
If Civic gets this right, then security will be improved in the aggregate, because there will only be one source of truth for PII, and that will be encrypted. The only way to unlock this data is to have the appropriate key, which would remain with the user.
Hackers focus their energy on large data silos, because they can get information about millions of people at once. If everyone had control of their own data, then there's no central repository to breach. Hacking one million people's data would instead involve hacking a million people, which is much more time consuming and less lucrative than spending some extra effort to do this millions of times at once.
The Civic token has earned the "OK" reputation by etherscan.io (the best reputation rating they give).
White paper The Civic white paper comes in at 18 pages and clearly explains the problem they are trying to solve. There isn't much that's too technical here, so I think most people should be able to read and understand it without having a background in tech.
One interesting thing about this project is that they are planning to work with Rootstock, or RSK . The cool thing about this is that once RSK goes live, smart contracts designed to run on Ethereum can be run on an interoperable layer connected to Bitcoin. Rootstock also will provide a scaling solution for Bitcoin, at this point too - exiting stuff!
If you want to know more about RSK, this video is a great place to start.
I like that Civic had a platform for identity before they got into blockchain. Their fund raising was to facilitate an expansion, but the domain expertise in identity was preexisting.
This diagram below is probably the most important one in the white paper.
Source: Civic whitepaper
What you're seeing here is the flow of the new "ecosystem," which is what Civic is calling their blockchain expansion. The user first submits documents to "Service provider A." An attestation record is created that can later be checked by "Service provider B," when the user interacts with them and requests verification.
A series of smart contracts ensure that best practices are followed, and that the marketplace for verification and attestation can interoperate. The data hash of the PII lives on the blockchain, where anyone can see that it exists. However, only an authorized party has access to the actual information.
Once these pieces are in place, information should be easy to verify, provided that authorization is given from the user's smartphone (confirmed with a finger print reader or otherwise).

Source: Twitter.com/civickey
Over on Reddit, their subscriber count is more modest.
Source: reddit.com/r/civicplatform

Criticism I don't really have any criticism for the project. But when it comes to the idea of investing in the token, I don't think that necessarily follows here.
First of all, there's ton of tokens, and there doesn't appear to be many users. With only $731k in daily volume, this token is thinly traded. Additionally, with the crypto winter being on, and only one-third of the tokens circulating from the total supply, we could see the price pushed further down.
The Civic token is the native currency of the platform, but that doesn't necessarily mean people are going to hang onto it to capture appreciation. Additionally, if users are rewarded with tokens just for using the platform, there will be a steady supply entering the market as new users join.
It kind of seems to me like everyone in the system is getting incentivized with these tokens, but where are the tokens coming from? If I understand correctly they are coming from the total supply.
I don't think the economic model of the token is really optimal for investing. Utility is baked in, but I think the incentive structure could have been implemented differently.
Conclusion Vinny Lingham, the CEO of Civic, is a popular figure in the cryptocurrency space. Gyft was a good step in the right direction, but that success doesn't guarantee that Civic will thrive.
The problems that Civic is taking on are challenging. Even solving a tiny piece of the digital identity puzzle would be meaningful (and possibly lucrative).
If Civic can build an amazing product, and they can build strategic partnerships, they will be in a good position. This is because I believe that blockchain tech is still in the very early stages. Also, because of the macro trends with information security and the shift to a digital society, leaders in the digital identity space will be able to capitalize on opportunities and capture market share when the time is right.
I think the need for digital identity is very clear today. It's possible that Civic could play a key role, and I intend to keep a close eye on their project.
